title: The Lost Compass of Valmora
subtitle: A compass that never points north, and a kingdom the world forgot
short_summary: Arhaan finds a silver compass that points not north but to whatever is lost, and follows it across the lake to Valmora, a silent mountain realm that has lost the very Echo that carried its voice to the world.

fingerprint.setting: Valmora, a forgotten mountain realm of turf-roofed stone houses and rope bridges beyond Mirecastle's lake
fingerprint.magical_object: A silver compass engraved with mountains that points to whatever is lost instead of north
fingerprint.problem: Valmora's Great Echo, which carried every message across the valleys and out into the world, has vanished, so the realm has fallen silent and been forgotten, even by the maps
fingerprint.antagonist_or_obstacle: The Tangle Pass, whose switchbacks rearrange themselves when unwatched, and a waterfall frozen solid by silence with the Echo trapped inside
fingerprint.ending: Arhaan goads the Echo into having the last word, freeing it; Valmora reappears in the school atlas marked 'Found by A.', the compass asks to be returned to its trunk, and the mountains call goodnight back to him across the lake

pages.heading: The Trunk Nobody Opened
pages.text:
At the back of Mirecastle Academy's library, past the shelves of sneezing dictionaries, stood a trunk that nobody ever opened. It had brass corners, a lid covered in faded luggage labels, and a sign that said PLEASE DO NOT, which was not even a complete sentence.

Arhaan had walked past it forty-one times. On the forty-second, he noticed the lid was not quite shut, and a thin golden light was leaking out of the gap like honey.

"Technically," he told himself, "the sign doesn't say what not to do." It was exactly the sort of reasoning that made House Viridian proud and librarians sigh. He lifted the lid.

pages.heading: A Needle With Opinions
pages.text:
Inside, wrapped in a moth-nibbled scarf, lay a compass. Its silver case was engraved with mountains, and its needle was not pointing north. It was pointing firmly at the floor beneath the Geography shelves. Around the rim, tiny letters read: I DO NOT FIND NORTH. I FIND WHAT IS LOST.

"Prove it," said Arhaan, who liked evidence. He crouched, followed the needle, and fished out a woolly green glove, slightly dusty. His own. Missing since the first frost of term.

"Right," he said, a little embarrassed. "Fair enough." The needle gave a small, smug wobble, then swung round to point out of the tall window, across the lake, towards the far blue mountains.

pages.heading: Planning, Not Rushing
pages.text:
A lesser adventurer might have sprinted straight out of the library. Arhaan made a list. He packed his notebook, two pencils (one for emergencies), a lantern, his green scarf with its silver serpent, three oat biscuits and the newly rescued glove.

Then he checked the old atlas by the window. Beyond the lake, the map showed only a smudge of grey and the words Here Be Nothing In Particular. "Nothing in particular," Arhaan murmured, "doesn't usually need a magic compass."

He rowed across the lake while the water lapped curiously at his oars, and climbed until the castle was a toy behind him. At the top of the first ridge the air shimmered like a curtain, and the needle trembled with excitement.

pages.heading: The Silent Kingdom
pages.text:
Arhaan stepped through the shimmer and into Valmora. It was astonishing, and very, very quiet. Stone houses with grassy roofs clung to the mountainsides. Rope bridges swung between the peaks. Waterfalls poured without a splash, and when a pebble rolled off the path, it landed without a sound.

Outside a little stone post office sat an elderly mountain goat in half-moon spectacles, sorting envelopes into a pigeonhole marked UNDELIVERED.

"A visitor!" the goat said. "Goodness. Nobody finds Valmora any more. Brindle, postmaster. Well, I was. Nothing's been sent in forty years." When Arhaan asked why, Brindle polished his spectacles sadly. "Because we lost our Echo."

pages.heading: How the Mountains Talked
pages.text:
Over a cup of mountain-flower tea, Brindle explained. In Valmora, nobody carried letters. You simply stood on your doorstep and read your letter aloud, and the Great Echo carried it valley to valley, all the way to whoever it was for. It even carried news beyond the mountains, so the whole world knew Valmora was there.

"Then one winter the Echo went wandering and never came back. Without it, no words could travel. And a place nobody hears from," Brindle sighed, "is a place everyone forgets. Even the maps."

Arhaan looked at the compass. The needle pointed up, up, towards the highest peak, where a pass zigzagged into the clouds. "I think," he said slowly, "I know what's lost."

pages.heading: The Tangle Pass
pages.text:
The path to the peak was called the Tangle Pass, and it had earned the name: its switchbacks shuffled themselves like playing cards whenever nobody was looking. Brindle came too, goats being excellent on steep paths, though he muttered about his knees.

Arhaan spotted a shortcut, a narrow ledge heading straight upward. "Much faster," he announced, and marched along it with great confidence. Ten minutes later he arrived back at the bottom, beside the same surprised-looking boulder. "Ah," said Brindle kindly. "The shortcuts are the worst ones."

Arhaan's ears went pink. Then he opened his notebook. "If the path moves when we don't look, then we look. You watch behind, I watch ahead, and I chalk an arrow at every turn." It was slow. It was careful. It worked.

pages.heading: A Waterfall of Glass
pages.text:
Near the summit they found a cave, and inside it a waterfall frozen solid, not with cold but with silence. It hung like a curtain of glass, and deep within it something glimmered and rippled, like a voice holding its breath.

"The Echo," breathed Brindle. "It must have wandered in here and got stuck." Arhaan knocked on the ice. Nothing. He shouted "Hello!" and the word dropped at his feet like a pebble. Brindle tried stamping, then recited a very long poem about turnips. The ice did not care in the slightest.

Arhaan sat down with an oat biscuit to think. Echoes, he reasoned, don't start conversations. They answer them. And "hello" wasn't really anything worth answering.

pages.heading: A Question Worth Answering
pages.text:
"What do echoes like best?" Arhaan asked. Brindle considered. "The last word. An echo simply cannot resist having the last word."

A slow, clever smile spread across Arhaan's face. He faced the frozen waterfall, took a deep breath and called, in his most provoking voice, "I bet you can't say Valmora!" For a moment, nothing. Then the ice gave a tiny crack. Something inside it fidgeted.

"I bet," Arhaan went on, "you've completely forgotten how!" The crack became a web of silver lines. Then the waterfall burst into sound, splashing and roaring, and out tumbled a great rolling voice, shouting "VALMORA! Valmora! valmora..." down every valley at once, as if it had been waiting forty years to prove somebody wrong.

pages.heading: The Post Goes Out
pages.text:
All across the mountains, Valmora woke up. Doors flew open. Bridges creaked. Waterfalls splashed, loudly and a little showily. A flock of cloud-goats bleated simply because they could.

Brindle hurried down to his post office faster than his knees had any right to allow, stood on the doorstep and read out the first letter in forty years: a birthday card for his sister, three valleys over. The Echo swept it away. A minute later, faintly, came the reply: "Thank you, Brindle! You're forty years late, you old goat!"

Brindle laughed until his spectacles fell off. "You didn't just find it," he told Arhaan. "You tricked it home." Arhaan shrugged. "Viridian," he said, and tried not to look too pleased. He did not entirely succeed.

pages.heading: Here Be Something Rather Particular
pages.text:
Back at Mirecastle, in the golden hour before supper, Arhaan opened the old atlas. The grey smudge had gone. In its place, in fresh ink, were peaks, bridges, a tiny post office and the word VALMORA in careful capitals. In the margin, in very small handwriting, someone had added: Found by A.

Then he held up the compass. Its needle swung round and pointed, quite decisively, at the old trunk. It wanted to be lost again, ready for whoever needed it next. Arhaan wrapped it in its scarf, tucked it away and added a note: Trust it. Mostly. Avoid shortcuts.

That night he leaned out of the Viridian tower and called, "Goodnight, Valmora!" And from far across the dark lake, the mountains called back.

title: The Whispering Woods
subtitle: Where every tree passes on a secret, and gets it a little bit wrong
short_summary: On Visiting Weekend, Arhaan and his sister Alysia explore Hushwater Wood, where the gossiping trees have muddled their chatter into a rumour of two axe-wielding giants, and the siblings must work together to set the whole forest straight.

fingerprint.setting: Hushwater Wood at the edge of Mirecastle's grounds, where trees pass whispers leaf to leaf, during Visiting Weekend
fingerprint.magical_object: The Grandmother Tree, the ancient oak where every whisper in the wood begins
fingerprint.problem: A harmless remark passed tree to tree has turned into a rumour of two giants with axes, terrifying the forest creatures, and any correction gets garbled too
fingerprint.antagonist_or_obstacle: The forest's own game of whispers, which twists words into what listeners fear, plus the Prickle Patrol of silver-quilled hedgehog guards
fingerprint.ending: The siblings send a laugh instead of words, which no whisper can twist; later a tree at home delivers Arhaan's secret message to Alysia, and she whispers one back

pages.heading: Visiting Weekend
pages.text:
Once a term, on Visiting Weekend, families were allowed up the winding road to Mirecastle Academy, and Arhaan's sister Alysia arrived like a small, determined weather system. Within an hour she had fed the lake ducks, raced a suit of armour down a corridor, and asked the Headmistress whether the castle had ever considered a slide.

"Show me something properly magical," she demanded. "Not lessons. Something real."

Arhaan considered. At the edge of the grounds, where the lawns gave up and the trees began, lay Hushwater Wood. "Come on," he said. "But stay close. The trees talk." Alysia's eyes went wide. "Talk about what?" Arhaan only grinned. "Everything."

pages.heading: Leaves With Something to Say
pages.text:
The moment they stepped under the branches, the whispering began. It rustled from leaf to leaf, soft as turning pages. Visitors... two of them... the small one has jam on her sleeve...

Alysia inspected her sleeve. "Rude," she told the nearest birch, "but accurate." They wandered deeper. Mushrooms glowed like nightlights. A stream giggled over pebbles. Bright eyes peeped from burrows and vanished again. "They're shy," said Arhaan. "Probably never seen a Viridian up close."

"Probably never seen your hair up close," said Alysia. But as they walked, the whispers began to change. They grew quicker and hissier, racing from tree to tree across the whole wood, and the words in them were not friendly at all.

pages.heading: Two Giants With a Plan
pages.text:
Giants, the trees whispered. Two giants... come to chop the forest... with axes and a plan... A rabbit bolted past. A hedgehog rolled itself into a ball so tight it bounced. High in the canopy, a family of lantern-moths switched off their glow all at once, as if someone had pulled a plug.

"Giants?" said Alysia, glancing about. Then she stopped. "Arhaan. I think they mean us." Arhaan replayed their walk in his head, the way he did with tricky puzzles. "At the edge of the wood, what did you say?"

Alysia frowned. "That I hoped we'd find pine cones to take home to Mum. And that you'd better have a plan." Arhaan groaned. "And the trees passed it along. Getting a little bit wronger every time."

pages.heading: A Very Clever Message
pages.text:
Alysia wanted to simply tell them the truth. "Leave it to me," said Arhaan. He cleared his throat and whispered into the nearest oak a beautifully precise message: "We are two friendly children visiting from Mirecastle Academy, with absolutely no axes and no intention of chopping anything, and we apologise for any confusion."

He was rather proud of it. The message rippled away through the wood. A minute later it came whispering back from the other direction: Blue kittens... from a muddy castle... absolutely all the axes... apologise to the chopping...

The woods erupted in alarmed squeaks. Somewhere, a badger fainted. Alysia patted his arm. "That," she said, "was too many words." Arhaan sighed. She was right, and it stung only a little.

pages.heading: Listening Properly
pages.text:
"Whispers get muddled the further they travel," Arhaan said, thinking hard. "So we can't fix it from here. We need to find where they start."

Alysia closed her eyes. She had always been the best listener in the family; she could hear the biscuit tin open from two rooms away. "They're not coming from everywhere," she said. "They're flowing, like a river. From that way."

She pointed down a mossy path neither of them had noticed. Arhaan checked it against the way the leaves leaned, the way the ferns bent, even the lichen on the stones. Every clue agreed. "You're brilliant," he said. Alysia nodded. "I know. Write that down."

pages.heading: The Prickle Patrol
pages.text:
The mossy path was guarded. Six hedgehog-like creatures with silvery quills stood shoulder to shoulder, bristling like a row of hairbrushes. The biggest one stamped a tiny foot.

"No giants past this point! We are the Prickle Patrol, and we are extremely pointy!" Arhaan crouched down so he was smaller than them. "Do we look like giants?" The prickle-hogs exchanged doubtful looks. "You look like giants who are crouching," said the leader.

Arhaan thought fast. If they couldn't go through the patrol, perhaps they could go over it. "Alysia," he whispered, "how's your tree-climbing?" Alysia grinned. She was, everyone agreed, the best climber in the family, and the one most often told to come down at once.

pages.heading: Over the Top
pages.text:
While Arhaan kept the Prickle Patrol busy with very serious questions about pointiness, and whether they had ever considered a patrol song, Alysia shinned up a leaning beech and edged along a branch that stretched right over their heads.

"It's wobbly," she called softly. "Very wobbly." Arhaan eyed the gaps like squares on a chessboard. "Next branch. The one with the knot," he whispered. "You've got it."

She dropped down on the far side as lightly as a leaf and held out a long trailing vine. Arhaan wished the patrol a very good afternoon, grabbed the vine and swung across in one clumsy, glorious arc, landing in a heap of ferns beside his sister. "Graceful," said Alysia. Arhaan picked a beetle out of his hair. "Strategic," he corrected.

pages.heading: The Grandmother Tree
pages.text:
At the heart of Hushwater Wood stood the oldest tree either of them had ever seen. Its trunk was as wide as a cottage, its roots curled like the backs of sleeping whales, and every whisper in the forest began in its creaking branches.

"Tell her something short," said Arhaan, remembering the blue kittens. "Too short to muddle." They tried. "Friends" came back as fiends. "No axes" came back as more axes. The creatures in the branches trembled.

Arhaan rubbed his forehead. "Words keep twisting into whatever everyone's already afraid of," he said. "We need to send something that can't turn scary." Alysia looked at him. He looked at her. And at exactly the same moment, they had exactly the same idea.

pages.heading: The Worst Impression in the World
pages.text:
"You'll have to make me laugh," said Alysia. "A real one. Not a polite one." Arhaan knew precisely what to do, because he had been perfecting it for years. He puffed out his cheeks, tucked his chin into his scarf, and performed his famous impression of a very pompous pigeon discovering a crumb.

Alysia snorted. Then she giggled. Then she laughed, a huge, helpless, hiccupping laugh that nobody could hear and stay frightened, and Arhaan laughed too, because hers always set him off.

The Grandmother Tree shook with it. The laugh raced from oak to ash to birch to beech, and no matter how many trees passed it on, a laugh stayed a laugh. The lantern-moths flickered back on. Rabbits peeped out. Somewhere in the distance, the Prickle Patrol was squeaking with giggles.

pages.heading: A Whisper Kept for Later
pages.text:
They walked out of the wood with pockets full of pine cones for Mum and a small hedgehog escort who insisted on pointing the way. By evening, Visiting Weekend was over. At the gate Alysia hugged Arhaan fiercely and climbed into the carriage home, grumbling that magic school was wasted on him.

What she didn't know was that, before they left, Arhaan had asked the Grandmother Tree to carry one message all the way to their garden, and to carry it herself, root to root, so not a word could slip.

That night, as Alysia opened her bedroom window, the old apple tree rustled softly. Your brother says: best climber in the family. Come back soon. Alysia smiled into the dark and whispered something back. It was very short. It did not get muddled at all.

title: The Clockwork Skyship
subtitle: A forgotten brass ship, a tangled sky, and one very clever plan
short_summary: Arhaan winds up a forgotten clockwork skyship in Mirecastle's attic and is carried into a knot of runaway winds around the castle's crooked weathercock. With gears, patience and a strategy of his own, he steers the ship home and delivers a letter that has waited a hundred years.

fingerprint.setting: The attic of Mirecastle's tallest tower and the windy sky around the castle spires
fingerprint.magical_object: The Periwinkle, a century-old clockwork skyship with a brass key and a music-box heart
fingerprint.problem: The skyship lifts off and is trapped circling the castle in a knot of tangled winds
fingerprint.antagonist_or_obstacle: The Great Weathercock, a giant brass bird on the highest spire, knocked crooked and spinning the winds into loops
fingerprint.ending: Arhaan straightens the weathercock, lands the ship, and finds a hundred-year-old letter from the ship's inventor inviting the next clever pair of hands to build something of their own

pages.heading: The Door Nobody Opened
pages.text:
At the very top of the West Tower of Mirecastle Academy, past the last lantern and the step that squeaked like a startled mouse, there was a small round door with a sign on it. The sign said: NOTHING IN HERE. PLEASE DO NOT CHECK.

Arhaan checked.

He was a Viridian, after all, and Viridians knew that a sign which works that hard to keep you out is usually guarding something worth seeing. He eased the door open. Dust drifted up like slow snow, and there, filling the whole attic from beam to beam, sat a ship. Not a boat for the lake. A ship with brass ribs, canvas wings folded like a sleeping moth's, and a painted name curling across its bow: the Periwinkle.

pages.heading: A Heart Made of Music
pages.text:
Arhaan walked all the way round it twice, the way his Tinkering tutor said you should look at any machine before touching it. There were gears the size of dinner plates and gears the size of shirt buttons. There was a steering wheel, a crank marked ALTITUDE, and a little glass window in the deck. Under the glass, a music box turned very slowly, playing three sleepy notes.

"You're clockwork," he whispered. "All of you."

Hanging from a hook by the wheel was a brass key as long as his forearm. Arhaan knew exactly what a sensible person would do next. A sensible person would go and fetch a teacher.

He decided to wind it just a little, only to hear what it sounded like.

pages.heading: Just a Little Too Much
pages.text:
One turn. The gears woke up and clicked like knitting needles. Two turns. The folded wings twitched. Three turns, four, five, and the music box began to play properly, a bright, bouncing tune that made the dust dance.

Arhaan should have stopped at five. He knew that later. But the tune was so cheerful, and the key turned so smoothly, that he gave it a sixth turn and a seventh, and on the seventh the attic roof, which turned out to be two great hatches, swung open all by itself.

The wings unfolded. The Periwinkle rose. And Arhaan, still holding the key, rose with it, out of the tower and into a sky full of evening gold.

pages.heading: Round and Round the Spires
pages.text:
For a whole glorious minute it was the best thing that had ever happened to him. The lake glittered below like a dropped mirror. Tiny students crossed the courtyard. A heron flapped past and gave him a very offended look.

Then the wind grabbed the ship.

It did not push it away or toss it about. It simply swung it round the East Spire, then round the Bell Tower, then round the East Spire again, like a toy on a string. Arhaan turned the wheel hard to the left. The ship went round to the right. He turned it to the right. The ship went round to the right, a bit faster.

"Right," said Arhaan, gripping the rail. "That's not ideal."

pages.heading: The Crooked Weathercock
pages.text:
On the fourth lap he noticed it. On top of the highest spire stood the Great Weathercock, a brass bird as big as a pony, whose job was to point politely at whichever way the wind blew. But someone, or something, had knocked it crooked. Its tail was jammed, its beak pointed at its own feet, and it was spinning in a stiff, grumpy circle.

Every time it spun, the wind spun with it.

"You're not showing the wind where to go," Arhaan realised. "You're telling it. And you've got it wrong."

The weathercock creaked at him, which he decided to take as an apology. Now all he needed was a way to reach it without the wind flinging him round the Bell Tower for the rest of his life.

pages.heading: Counting the Wind
pages.text:
Fighting the wind had not worked, so Arhaan stopped fighting and started watching. He sat cross-legged on the deck and counted.

The gusts came in a pattern. Strong, strong, strong, strong, strong, strong, and then, just for a heartbeat, nothing at all, a tiny pocket of stillness while the weathercock's stiff tail clunked round its circle. Then six strong gusts again.

"Seven beats," he murmured. "Six pushes and one pause."

He looked down through the glass at the music box. Its tune also had a rhythm, a happy, bouncing rhythm of eight beats, and every gear on the ship was marching along to it. That was the problem. The Periwinkle was dancing to the wrong song.

pages.heading: A Gear for a Gear
pages.text:
Arhaan lifted the glass lid. Inside, the music box's comb was plucked by a brass cylinder dotted with tiny pins. One pin, he saw, had been added later and soldered on a bit wonkily, as if the inventor had wanted a jollier tune.

He did not have a toolkit. He did have the heavy brass key, a hair clip he had borrowed from the lost property box and never returned, and a great deal of determination. Carefully, very carefully, he used the clip to nudge the wonky pin off its perch.

The tune stumbled, hiccupped, and settled into something slower. Six notes and a rest. Six notes and a rest.

The ship's gears changed step. Beneath his feet, the whole Periwinkle seemed to relax.

pages.heading: Riding the Pause
pages.text:
Now the ship and the wind were keeping the same time, and Arhaan could plan. He would not steer during the gusts. He would wait, like a cat waiting for a door to open, and steer only in the pause.

Gust, gust, gust, gust, gust, gust. Pause. He turned the wheel one notch and the ship slid a little closer to the spire.

Gust, gust, gust, gust, gust, gust. Pause. Another notch. He wound the ALTITUDE crank half a turn and the ship rose level with the weathercock's jammed brass tail.

"Nearly," he said. His hands were shaking a bit. That was fine. Brave people's hands shook too; they just kept steering.

pages.heading: A Nudge in the Right Direction
pages.text:
Under the bow hung a small anchor on a chain, meant for tying up to tower tops. Arhaan let it down, link by clinking link, until it dangled just beside the weathercock's tail.

He waited for the pause. Then he swung the chain, once, gently, the way you nudge a stuck drawer rather than yanking it.

The anchor tapped the tail. Something inside went clunk. The weathercock shivered, lifted its beak, and swung round smoothly to point west, exactly where the evening breeze was coming from.

All at once the sky untangled. The winds stopped looping and began to flow, soft and straight, like a river remembering which way the sea is. The Periwinkle bobbed gratefully on top of them.

pages.heading: The Letter in the Hold
pages.text:
Landing turned out to be easy once the sky was behaving. Arhaan wound the crank down, notch by patient notch, and the Periwinkle settled back into its attic like a hen onto a nest. The roof hatches creaked shut. The music box played its six notes and a rest, then fell quiet.

In the silence he heard a soft flump. A small drawer in the steering column had popped open. Inside lay a letter, yellow as old butter, sealed with a wax cog.

It was addressed: To whoever makes her fly again.

Arhaan checked the sign on the door behind him, which still said NOTHING IN HERE. Then he broke the seal.

pages.heading: Something of Your Own
pages.text:
The letter was short, in tidy, looping handwriting.

If you are reading this, you were curious enough to open a door you were told not to, and clever enough to come back down. I made the Periwinkle to carry letters between the towers. She did well, but I always meant to build something better. I never did. Perhaps you will.

Tucked inside was a single brass cog, no bigger than a coin, and a blank sheet of drawing paper.

Arhaan sat on the dusty attic floor for a long time, turning the cog in his fingers while the sun went down. Then he took out his pencil, smoothed the paper flat on the ship's deck, and began to draw.

title: Tito's Magical Mishap
subtitle: One uncle, one cauldron, and far too many moustaches
short_summary: Uncle Tito visits Mirecastle and brews a tonic to make his moustache magnificent, but a pinch of the wrong herb means everything he touches while laughing sprouts one of its own. Arhaan has to find a way to stop the most laughing uncle in the world from laughing.

fingerprint.setting: Mirecastle Academy's Visitors' Parlour and corridors on Family Afternoon
fingerprint.magical_object: Tito's travelling cauldron and his home-made Magnificence Tonic
fingerprint.problem: A pinch of Gigglewort in the tonic makes anything Tito touches while laughing sprout a moustache
fingerprint.antagonist_or_obstacle: Tito's own unstoppable laughter, which makes the moustaches multiply
fingerprint.ending: Arhaan breaks the spell with a joke so unfunny that Tito finally stops laughing, but the stern portrait of the founder refuses to give her new moustache back

pages.heading: Uncle Tito Arrives Loudly
pages.text:
You always knew when Uncle Tito had arrived, because something fell over. On Family Afternoon at Mirecastle Academy, it was a coat stand, a potted fern and, very nearly, the Deputy Head.

"Arhaan!" Tito boomed, sweeping him into a hug that smelled of peppermint and bonfire smoke. "Look at you! Taller! Cleverer! Greener! Is that the Viridian scarf? Very smart. Very serpenty."

He was wearing a purple travelling cloak, odd socks, and an expression Arhaan knew well. It was the expression of a man with a Plan.

"I've brought a present," said Tito, patting a lumpy bag that clanked. "Well. Half a present. The other half I'm going to make, right here, in front of you."

pages.heading: The Magnificence Tonic
pages.text:
The Visitors' Parlour was a quiet, polite room with velvet chairs, a ticking clock and a large portrait of the Academy's founder, Dame Ottoline Mire, who looked as though she had never laughed in her life and did not intend to start.

Tito pulled a small copper cauldron out of his bag and set it on the tea table.

"Magnificence Tonic," he announced. "My own recipe. One sip and your moustache becomes truly magnificent. Glossy. Curly at the ends. The sort of moustache people write poems about."

"You don't have a moustache," said Arhaan.

"Exactly," said Tito, beaming. "Which is why I need a magnificent one."

Arhaan could not argue with that sort of logic, so he passed him the matches.

pages.heading: Parsley, Probably
pages.text:
Tito cooked the way he did everything else: enthusiastically and slightly on fire. In went a spoonful of honey, three drops of rosewater, a comb, for inspiration, and a crushed silver beetle shell.

"Now a pinch of parsley," he said, rummaging. "Parsley, parsley... here we are."

Arhaan peered at the little jar. The leaves were pink and curly and appeared to be quietly giggling.

"Tito, I don't think parsley giggles."

"Nonsense. It's fresh parsley. That's why it's cheerful." In went the pinch. The cauldron gave a loud hiccup, a puff of pink steam, and a sound exactly like someone trying not to snort in a library.

Tito drank a large spoonful, smacked his lips, and waited.

pages.heading: The Kettle Grows Up
pages.text:
Nothing happened to Tito's lip. It stayed exactly as bare as before.

"Hm," said Tito. "Slow-acting." He reached for the teapot to pour himself a comforting cup, noticed that he had put the sugar bowl on his head at some point, and burst out laughing.

The teapot sprouted a moustache.

It was a big one. Black, bushy and curled at the tips, sitting just under the spout as if it had always been there. The teapot looked extremely distinguished.

Tito stared. Then, because he was Tito, he laughed even harder, clapping Arhaan on the shoulder, and Arhaan felt something tickle his top lip.

He looked cross-eyed. He had a moustache. It was ginger.

pages.heading: A Most Distinguished Afternoon
pages.text:
"Stop laughing!" said Arhaan.

"I can't!" wheezed Tito. "You look like a sea captain!" He slapped the arm of a velvet chair. The chair grew a moustache. He leaned on the clock. The clock grew a moustache, which bounced every time it ticked. He wiped a tear of laughter from his eye with a napkin, and the napkin grew one too and fluttered away like a very hairy butterfly.

Out in the corridor, a first-year shrieked with delight. A suit of armour had a handlebar moustache poking through its visor. Somebody's cat stalked past looking outraged and considerably more whiskery than usual.

Arhaan pulled the jar of "parsley" out of Tito's bag and read the tiny label on the bottom. It said: GIGGLEWORT.

pages.heading: What the Label Said
pages.text:
Arhaan turned the jar round and read the small print, the way Viridians always read the small print.

GIGGLEWORT. Adds cheer to any brew. WARNING: if brewed with growing charms, the drinker's laughter will pass the growth to whatever they are touching. Effect ends only when the drinker hears a joke that is truly, completely unfunny, and does not laugh.

Arhaan looked up. Across the parlour, Tito was laughing so hard at the moustached teapot that he had to hold onto the fireplace. The fireplace grew a moustache.

This was a problem. Tito laughed at everything. He laughed at clouds. He laughed at spoons. He had once laughed for four minutes at the word "wobble."

Finding a joke Tito would not laugh at was going to take a strategy.

pages.heading: Plan A Does Not Go Well
pages.text:
Arhaan's first plan was simple. Keep Tito's hands still, so at least nothing new would grow.

"Uncle, sit on your hands," he said.

Tito sat on his hands, which he found hilarious, and the velvet cushion beneath him grew a moustache so enormous it lifted him slightly off the seat. He laughed at that. Then he laughed at himself laughing.

Arhaan tried a joke next, just to test the waters. "Why don't skeletons fight each other? They haven't got the guts."

That was a mistake. Tito howled. He flung out both arms, and every single portrait along the parlour wall sprouted a moustache at once, including, with a soft and terrible fwump, Dame Ottoline Mire.

The founder's eyebrows went up. Her new moustache went up with them.

pages.heading: Thinking Like a Viridian
pages.text:
Arhaan sat down on the only chair without facial hair and made himself think.

Funny jokes were no good. Tito loved them. Silly things were no good. Tito loved those even more. What Tito could not stand, Arhaan remembered, was being left hanging. At birthday parties he always wanted to know how every story ended. He read the last page of books first. He once rang Arhaan's mother at midnight to ask how a crossword clue worked out.

A joke that went nowhere. A joke with no ending at all. That might just be unfunny enough.

Arhaan straightened his ginger moustache, which helped him feel serious, and walked over to his uncle.

pages.heading: The Least Funny Joke in the World
pages.text:
"Tito," he said gravely. "I've got a joke."

Tito wiped his eyes. "Go on, go on."

"Why did the teapot cross the corridor?"

Tito leaned in, grinning, ready to explode. "I don't know! Why did the teapot cross the corridor?"

Arhaan looked at him steadily. "It just did."

There was a long pause. Tito's grin wobbled. His eyebrows gathered together in confusion. He opened his mouth, then shut it. "That's... that's not a joke," he said slowly. "There's no reason. Where's the funny bit?"

"There isn't one."

Tito frowned, deeply and genuinely offended. And for the first time all afternoon, he did not laugh at all.

pages.heading: The Great Moustache Migration
pages.text:
All over the castle, the moustaches let go.

They floated up off the teapot, the clock, the chairs, the armour and the extremely relieved cat, drifting through the air like fluffy dandelion seeds. Arhaan's ginger one tickled free and bobbed away out of the window. A great cloud of them sailed out over the lake, where a family of ducks looked up in puzzlement.

Tito let out a long breath and sat down heavily. "I still don't get that joke," he muttered.

"That's the point," said Arhaan.

"Well, I don't like it," said Tito. Then he looked at the empty cauldron, and at the flustered, bare-lipped teapot, and his mouth twitched. Arhaan put a firm hand over it, just in case.

pages.heading: Dame Ottoline Keeps Hers
pages.text:
Every moustache in Mirecastle had floated away. Every single one, except one.

Above the fireplace, Dame Ottoline Mire still wore hers: a splendid silver thing that curled at both ends. As Arhaan and Tito watched, she lifted one painted hand and gave it a small, satisfied twirl.

"Madam," said Tito politely, "I believe that belongs to me."

The founder looked down at him with great dignity, and did not give it back.

Tito packed up his cauldron, promised to label his jars properly, and left the Gigglewort with Arhaan for safekeeping. It is still in a locked drawer in the Viridian dormitory, and on quiet evenings, if you press your ear to the wood, you can hear it chuckling.

title: The Shadow in the Library
subtitle: A night-time mystery on the shelves of Mirecastle
short_summary: A shadow is roaming the Mirecastle Academy library after dark, and Arhaan is determined to find out why. What he discovers needs a gentle hand far more than a clever trap.

fingerprint.magical_object: an old gilded storybook, The Tales of Hollow Hill
fingerprint.problem: a shadow is roaming the shelves, snuffing lamps and moving books
fingerprint.antagonist_or_obstacle: a frightened ink hare escaped from an illustration, and a misfiled book it cannot find because it cannot read
fingerprint.ending: the hare returns to its page, which now shows Arhaan drawn beside it; the book is kept quietly by the librarian's low lamp

pages.heading: Whispers at Breakfast
pages.text:
By Thursday, the whole of Mirecastle Academy was talking about the shadow in the library. "It walks along the top shelves," said a boy from House Amberlight, spilling his porridge. "No person attached. Just the shadow."

A girl across the table added that it had blown out every lamp in the poetry aisle, and moved all the atlases, and possibly sneezed, though she wasn't certain shadows could.

Arhaan buttered his toast slowly and said nothing, which is what Viridians do when they are thinking very hard. A mystery that nobody had solved was, in his opinion, a mystery waiting for the right person. He had a strong suspicion about who that person might be.

pages.heading: The Lamp-Keeper's Job
pages.text:
The librarian, Mistress Ashgrove, was a tall woman with silver spectacles and a cardigan that had more pockets than any cardigan strictly needs. "Nobody wants to stay late any more," she sighed. "I need someone to trim the lamps after supper."

"I'll do it," said Arhaan, a little too quickly. Mistress Ashgrove peered at him and asked whether he might be hoping to meet their visitor. Arhaan considered fibbing, then considered how clever she looked, and decided against it. "Only a bit," he admitted.

To his surprise, she smiled. "Then bring a notebook. Curiosity without notes is just nosiness."

pages.heading: A Map of Sightings
pages.text:
Arhaan's notebook filled up quickly. Every evening he trimmed the lamps and asked the older students what they had seen, and when, and exactly where. Then he drew a map of the library and marked each sighting with a small silver dot.

The dots were not random. They began at the atlases, crept through astronomy, wandered past bees and bridges, and stopped last night beside cookery.

"A, B, C," Arhaan whispered, and a shiver of excitement ran all the way down to his shoelaces. "It's going through the alphabet. It's looking for something." Tonight, by his reckoning, the shadow would reach the letter D.

pages.heading: The Clever Trap
pages.text:
Arhaan had a plan, and it was, he felt, an excellent plan. He would hide behind the dictionaries with the brightest lantern in the library, and the moment the shadow appeared, he would flood it with light. You cannot hide a shadow from a lantern. Everyone knows that.

At a quarter past nine, the lamps along the D shelves flickered. A shape slid down the spines of the books: long ears, a narrow nose, four quick legs. Arhaan leapt out. "Got you!"

The lantern blazed. The shadow gave a tiny, papery gasp, shrank to the size of a thumbprint and vanished beneath a bookcase. The library went very quiet, and Arhaan suddenly felt rather large and rather loud.

pages.heading: What the Light Showed
pages.text:
He knelt down and peered under the bookcase. Something small was trembling there, flat as a paper cut-out and dark as ink. "Oh," said Arhaan softly. "You're not a spooky shadow at all. You're frightened."

He set the lantern behind him so its light fell away from the bookcase, and sat down cross-legged on the cold floor. A good strategist, he reminded himself, knows when a plan has gone wrong and makes a new one. The new plan was simply to wait.

It took a long time, and his foot went to sleep. But at last the little dark shape edged out, one ear and then the other, and he could see what it really was: a hare, made entirely of ink.

pages.heading: The Hare Who Could Not Read
pages.text:
Up close, the hare had fine lines for whiskers and neat cross-hatching along its back, the way pictures do in very old books. It pointed one paw at the shelves, then drooped.

"You've come out of a book," Arhaan said slowly, "and you can't find your way back in." The hare nodded so hard its ears flapped. Suddenly the alphabet made sense. The hare had been searching shelf by shelf, but it could not read the titles. It was guessing from the covers, and a library has an awful lot of covers.

"Right," said Arhaan, cracking his knuckles. "Luckily, I can read. Let's think about this properly."

pages.heading: Clues in the Ink
pages.text:
Arhaan studied the hare the way he would study a riddle. Its lines were brown-black, not blue, which meant old ink. There was a faint gold edge around its ears, as if it had once been printed beside gilded lettering. And on its left hind foot was a tiny smudge, like a fingerprint left by some eager reader long ago.

"Old book, gold letters, and somebody touched this page a lot," he muttered. "So it was a favourite."

He opened the library's great ledger, which recorded every book ever borrowed, and ran his finger down the columns. It stopped at the title borrowed more than any other, three hundred years ago: The Tales of Hollow Hill, with gilded pictures.

pages.heading: Misplaced
pages.text:
The ledger said The Tales of Hollow Hill belonged under T. Arhaan and the hare hurried there together, the hare bounding along the edge of the shelves like a dark ribbon. The book was not there.

Arhaan's heart sank for a moment, and then he grinned, because he had spotted something else. A repair label had been glued over one spine on the shelf below, and in brand-new lettering it read: Hollow Hill, Tales of.

"Somebody rebound it and filed it under H," he said. "No wonder you couldn't find it. You'd never get there by guessing." The hare stared at the spine, then did a little leap that was very nearly a somersault.

pages.heading: Home Between the Pages
pages.text:
Arhaan eased the book from the shelf and let it fall open on the reading table. Halfway through, there was a picture of a green hill under a round moon, and in the middle of the picture was an empty space exactly the shape of a hare.

The ink hare looked up at him and touched his hand with one cool paw, light as a page turning. Then it hopped onto the paper and settled into its space. Its lines sharpened, its gold edges shone, and it was a picture again, as if it had never left.

Arhaan let out a long breath he had not noticed he was holding.

pages.heading: A New Illustration
pages.text:
He was about to close the book when something made him look again. The moon was still round and the hill was still green, and the hare was still in the middle. But now, sitting beside it in the grass, drawn in the same old brown ink with a faint gold edge, was a small boy with a notebook on his knee.

Arhaan did not tell the whole school. He told Mistress Ashgrove, who listened carefully, then quietly moved The Tales of Hollow Hill to the shelf beside her desk, where the lamp was always kept low.

And sometimes, when the library was empty, Arhaan would open it to that page, just to check that both of them were still there.

title: The Island of Singing Creatures
subtitle: A sea voyage, a broken song and one missing note
short_summary: Arhaan and Uncle Tito follow a song through the fog to a hidden island where every creature speaks in music. The island's Tide Song has lost its final note, and only Arhaan can work out how to find it.

fingerprint.setting: a hidden island in the fog with a coral-walled lagoon
fingerprint.magical_object: an empty lemonade bottle tuned with seawater
fingerprint.problem: the Tide Song that opens the lagoon keeps breaking, so baby harp-turtles cannot reach the sea
fingerprint.antagonist_or_obstacle: a musical puzzle: the song's lowest note is missing because the old turtle Oolu's shell is cracked
fingerprint.ending: the turtles swim free and the creatures add two notes to their song, one for Arhaan and a gloriously off-key one for Tito; the bottle hums on Arhaan's windowsill

pages.heading: A Boat Called Marmalade
pages.text:
Uncle Tito arrived at the harbour wearing a captain's hat three sizes too big and carrying a picnic basket that clinked suspiciously. "Behold," he announced, sweeping an arm towards a small orange boat, "the Marmalade! Borrowed from a friend. Mostly waterproof."

When Arhaan asked what mostly meant, Tito explained that the leaky bit was at the back, so they would simply sit at the front. Arhaan climbed aboard anyway, because a day at sea with Tito was never boring.

"Fishermen round here say there's an island that sings," Tito said, winking. "Nobody can find it. Which is exactly why we're going to."

pages.heading: Singing in the Fog
pages.text:
By noon the sea had turned silver and the fog rolled in, thick as porridge. Tito tried to read the map upside down, then sideways, then gave up and ate a toffee.

Then Arhaan heard it. Far away, faint as a kettle in another room, came a thread of music: three high notes, then two middle ones, then something deeper. Tito stopped chewing. "Well, I never. Is that a song, or my stomach?"

"It's a song," said Arhaan, pointing, "and it keeps coming from the same direction." Tito, who trusted his nephew's ears far more than his own map-reading, turned the Marmalade towards the music.

pages.heading: The Hidden Island
pages.text:
The fog thinned like a curtain being drawn, and there it was: a round green island with pale cliffs and a still blue lagoon in its middle, ringed by a wall of pink coral. And the island was full of singers. Tiny blue birds whistled on the rocks, plump furry creatures with whiskers hummed on the sand, and crabs clicked and chimed along the tideline like little bells.

Nobody spoke. Everybody sang. When a bird wanted a crab to move, it trilled. When the crab refused, it clicked back something that sounded distinctly rude.

"Marvellous," breathed Tito. "I'm going to sing hello." Arhaan said please don't, but it was already too late.

pages.heading: Tito Says Hello
pages.text:
Tito's singing voice sounded like a goose trying to open a jar. Every creature on the beach stopped and stared. Then, to Arhaan's great relief, the furry creatures began to laugh, a chuckling, bubbling laugh that rippled across the sand until even the crabs were rattling their claws.

"Tough crowd," said Tito, beaming. "But warm."

One of the furry creatures waddled up to Arhaan and looked at him with big, worried eyes. It hummed a short phrase, then pointed a flipper towards the lagoon, where the coral wall stood closed and tight. Behind it, dozens of tiny shelled heads bobbed in the water, waiting.

pages.heading: The Song That Stopped
pages.text:
It took a lot of pointing, humming and drawing in the sand, but at last Arhaan understood. Every evening, the creatures sang the Tide Song. When it was sung all the way through, the coral wall opened and the sea rushed into the lagoon.

Tonight was special, because the baby harp-turtles who had hatched in the lagoon were ready to swim out into the ocean for the very first time. But the song kept breaking. Every evening it reached the last line and simply stopped.

"So the gate stays shut," said Arhaan, "and the babies can't leave." The furry creature nodded sadly and hummed a single, hopeless note.

pages.heading: Grandmother Oolu
pages.text:
At the edge of the lagoon lay the biggest turtle Arhaan had ever seen. Her shell was ridged like the strings of a harp, and when the breeze passed over it, the ridges hummed. Except for one. A long crack ran across the lowest ridge, and where there should have been a note, there was only a dry, whispery rattle.

"Poor old girl," said Tito gently, patting her shell. "Storm damage, I'd say." The turtle, whom the others sang of as Oolu, blinked one slow, ancient eye at them.

Arhaan sat down on the sand. "Sing it again," he asked the creatures. "The whole song. I need to hear exactly where it goes wrong."

pages.heading: Steps Going Down
pages.text:
So they sang, and Arhaan closed his eyes and listened the way he listened to a tricky lesson. The birds sang first, highest of all. Then the furry ones, a step lower. Then the crabs, a step lower again. Each line climbed down, like someone walking down a staircase one careful step at a time. And at the bottom, where the final step should have been, there was silence, and every creature turned to look at Oolu.

"It's a staircase," said Arhaan, opening his eyes, "and the last step is missing. We need one note, lower than the crabs."

Tito offered to sing it. Arhaan asked, very politely, whether he could sing in tune. Tito thought about it honestly and said no.

pages.heading: The Bottle Plan
pages.text:
Arhaan tried himself, but his voice squeaked long before it got deep enough. He frowned at the sea, and the sea gave him an idea. "Tito, what's clinking in the picnic basket?"

Tito produced three empty lemonade bottles, looking faintly guilty. Arhaan filled one to the brim with seawater, put his lips to the top and blew across it. Out came a thin, piercing whistle, and every crab on the beach sneezed and fell over sideways.

"Too high! Sorry, sorry!" cried Arhaan, going red. Then he remembered a science lesson. Less water meant more air inside, and more air meant a deeper note. He had got it exactly backwards.

pages.heading: Tuning the Tide
pages.text:
Arhaan poured a little water out and blew. Lower. He poured out more. Lower still. The furry creatures leaned in, humming encouragement, and the crabs picked themselves up and clicked approvingly each time he came closer.

At last, with only a finger's depth of water left, the bottle gave a deep, round, rumbling note, and Oolu lifted her enormous head. "That's it," whispered Tito. "That's her note." He had quietly pressed three of his emergency toffees into the crack on her shell. "Just a patch," he explained, "until it heals."

The sun touched the sea. The birds took a breath, and the Tide Song began.

pages.heading: The Last Step
pages.text:
Down the staircase went the song: the birds, the furry ones, the crabs, each step lower and richer than the one before. When the silence came, Arhaan was ready. He blew across the bottle, long and steady, and the deep note rolled out across the lagoon.

For a moment nothing happened. Then, very slowly, the coral wall parted like two hands opening, and the sea poured in, bright and fizzing. Out swam the baby harp-turtles, dozens of them, their tiny shells humming like a box of little bells.

Arhaan kept blowing until his cheeks ached. He did not want to miss a single one.

pages.heading: Tito's Verse
pages.text:
As they sailed away in the dusk, the creatures lined the beach and sang to them, and the song had changed. At the very end came a deep, round note, exactly like the bottle, and Arhaan knew that one was his. Then came a second note, wobbly, wildly out of tune and extremely loud, sung by every creature at once.

Tito put a hand on his heart. "They've put me in the song," he said, deeply moved. "They've got my voice perfectly."

Arhaan laughed so hard the Marmalade rocked, and behind them the fog drew closed and the island was gone. But the bottle still sits on his windowsill at Mirecastle, and whenever the wind blows in from the sea, it hums one low note.

title: The Moonstone Promise
subtitle: A promise sixty years late, and one hour of eclipse to keep it
short_summary: On the night of a total eclipse, Arhaan and Alysia find a glowing moonstone and a note asking a stranger to keep a promise made long ago. With the moon's shadow ticking away inside the stone, they must cross the lake's vanishing Moon Stair before the eclipse ends.

fingerprint.setting: Mirecastle Academy's Lantern Tower and a stair of glowing stones rising across the castle lake during a total lunar eclipse
fingerprint.magical_object: A moonstone whose inner silver line counts down the minutes of the eclipse and makes time slip and stutter around it
fingerprint.problem: A promise to return the moonstone to the lake, made by a frightened student in 1961 and never kept, must be fulfilled before the eclipse ends
fingerprint.antagonist_or_obstacle: The Moon Stair, whose stones only hold the weight of people speaking promises they have truly kept, and rewind anyone who fibs
fingerprint.ending: The old ferry-keeper who made the original promise crosses with them to keep it herself; the Moon-Heron takes the stone, and Arhaan keeps a smaller promise to his sister by giving her the first look at the returning moon through a spyglass

pages.heading: The Night of the Hollow Moon
pages.text:
Once every few years, the moon over Mirecastle Academy slipped into the Earth's shadow and turned the colour of a ripe plum. The students called it the Hollow Moon, and on those nights the whole castle held its breath.

Arhaan had planned for it for weeks. He had volunteered to polish the great telescope in the Lantern Tower, which was dull work, but it came with a key. A key meant the best view in the castle. That was the Viridian way: think three moves ahead.

"You promised I'd get the first look," said Alysia, trotting up the spiral stairs behind him.

"I did," said Arhaan grandly. "Word of a Viridian."

pages.heading: The Stone Behind the Stone
pages.text:
The tower room smelled of brass and old dust. As the first bite of shadow crept across the moon, one stone in the wall began to glow, faintly, like a lamp left on in another room.

Arhaan prised it loose. Behind it sat a small tin, and inside the tin lay a moonstone the size of a plum stone, milky and cool. Beside it was a note in careful, looping handwriting.

"I promised the Lake I would bring this back on the next night the moon went hollow," Alysia read aloud. "But I was frightened of the Moon Stair, and I did not go. If you find this, please keep my promise for me. W. A., Autumn 1961."

Inside the moonstone, a thin silver line had begun to move.

pages.heading: Time Goes Wobbly
pages.text:
"It's counting," said Arhaan, holding the stone up. "Look. The line is sliding round like a clock hand. I think it's counting down the eclipse."

Then time did something odd. The tower clock struck nine, then struck nine again, then thought better of it and struck half past eight. A candle flame shrank backwards into its wick and popped out again.

"Did I just say something?" asked Alysia. "I think I just said something."

"Did I just say something?" she asked again, and frowned.

Arhaan pocketed the stone quickly, and the room steadied. "Right," he said. "The stone is impatient. It wants to go home, and we have until the moon comes back."

pages.heading: A Shortcut, More or Less
pages.text:
The lake was a long way down. The main staircase would take ages, and the Prefects would ask questions that took even longer.

"The laundry chute," Arhaan announced. "It goes straight to the ground floor. I worked it out from the plans in the library. The boathouse is just beyond it."

He was right about the chute and wrong about where it came out. They shot down in a whoosh of pillowcases and landed, with great dignity, in a bin of kitchen potatoes.

Alysia picked a potato out of her hair. "Very strategic."

"It's still quicker," said Arhaan, who refused to be defeated by vegetables. And, to be fair, it was.

pages.heading: The Moon Stair Rises
pages.text:
Out on the shore, the lake lay flat and dark as a sheet of glass. Then, as the last curve of moonlight vanished, something rose from the water.

Stepping stones, one after another, each glowing softly silver, curving out towards the middle of the lake where a single tall stone waited like a lectern.

Alysia took a step backwards. She did not like dark water, not even a little.

"I'll hold your hand the whole way," Arhaan said. "I promise."

She looked at him for a long moment, as if weighing the words. Then she slid her hand into his, and together they stepped onto the first stone.

pages.heading: The Stair Knows
pages.text:
The stone hummed under their feet, and a voice as soft as ripples spoke from nowhere in particular: "A promise kept, to take a step."

"I promised to feed Mrs Crumble's toad while she was away," said Alysia, "and I did." The next stone brightened, and they stepped forward.

Arhaan cleared his throat. "I promised Mother I'd keep my trunk tidy."

The stair gave a small, disapproving wobble, and time folded like a page. Suddenly they were back on the first stone, the silver line in the moonstone a little further along.

"You shoved everything under your bed," said Alysia.

"That is a form of tidy," said Arhaan, but he was already choosing his next promise more carefully.

pages.heading: Stone by Stone
pages.text:
After that, Arhaan played it cleverly. He only offered promises he had truly kept, and he kept them short so as not to waste time. He had promised to return a library book, and had. He had promised his friend Tamsin he would not tell anyone about her fear of pigeons, and had not, not even now.

Alysia matched him stone for stone. The stair glowed brighter with every true word, and the far pillar drew closer.

But the silver line in the moonstone was sliding faster now. At the very edge of the dark moon, a thin rim of light was beginning to return.

And the last stone before the pillar had not risen at all.

pages.heading: The Missing Step
pages.text:
"A promise kept, to take a step," the stair whispered again, but no promise they offered would raise that final stone.

Arhaan thought hard. It was not their promise to keep. They had only borrowed it. The stair wanted the person who had made it.

Then came the creak of oars. Out of the dark slid the ferry-keeper's little boat, and in it sat old Mrs Ashby, who rowed visitors across the lake and grumbled about everything. Her lantern shook in her hand.

"I saw the stone glowing from my window," she said quietly. "I haven't seen that light since I was your age."

Arhaan looked at the note. W. A. "Wren Ashby," he said.

pages.heading: Sixty Years Late
pages.text:
"I was so frightened," said Mrs Ashby. "I told myself I'd go next time. And then next time was sixty years away, and I stopped believing I could."

Arhaan held out the moonstone. He had wanted, very badly, to be the one who placed it. It would have been a splendid thing to tell everyone. But it was not his promise.

"You don't have to do it alone," he said. "That's rather the point of company."

Mrs Ashby stepped from her boat onto the stair. "I promised the Lake I would bring this back," she said, her voice steadier than her hands. The last stone rose beneath her like a held breath let go, and the three of them reached the pillar together.

pages.heading: The First Look
pages.text:
From the pillar rose a heron made of moonlight, tall and silver and in no hurry at all. It bowed to Mrs Ashby, took the moonstone gently in its beak, and slipped beneath the water. The moon's reflection bloomed on the lake a heartbeat before the moon itself returned to the sky.

Mrs Ashby laughed, a young, surprised sound. "Better late," she said, wiping her eyes.

Then Arhaan's face fell. "The telescope. I promised you the first look." He hesitated, then spotted a brass spyglass rolling in the bottom of the boat. He handed it to Alysia just as the last sliver of shadow slid away.

Alysia looked first, as promised. And Arhaan, beside her, found he didn't mind being second at all.
